title: Prajna Paramita
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: The talk's main teaching is that wisdom (prajna) is a way of being that allows us to face life's challenges with integrity, composure, and skillful response. It develops from understanding the fundamental teachings of Buddhism, particularly emptiness and impermanence, which reveal the interconnectedness of all phenomena and our place within it. By embracing this understanding, we can cultivate wisdom and navigate life's uncertainties with greater ease, humility, and compassion, ultimately finding peace and freedom in the midst of chaos.

Wright is an academic, a professor of Asian religions in Southern California, and he's interested in how Zen Buddhism and Buddhist ideas apply in modern life.
Norman Fischer, our founding teacher, is also really interested in how we moderns practice Buddhism in daily life.

These all can be practiced without being wise, but they lead to wisdom and become infused with wisdom.
So they're both the result of wisdom and the cause of becoming wise.
Dale Wright says, *wisdom is not just a matter of having knowledge, though knowledge is necessary for developing wisdom, and experience is also necessary.
Wisdom is a certain comportment, a particular way of being in the world, rather than a doctrinal or conceptual view or idea.* A certain comportment, a way of acting and being in the world.
And what is that way?
I hope to outline that in the talk today, and also in the next few definitions I'll say a little bit more in detail about what this comportment will be.
*First of all, viewing the world in a certain way leads to wisdom.
That way, wisdom is the ability to face the truth and not be unnerved or frightened.*
That's a watchword for us today: face the truth and not be unnerved or frightened.
Another one is, *it is the capacity to be disillusioned, but not disheartened.* I like that one.
Disillusion, meaning let go of one's illusions.
Disillusion feels like it's a sad, grumpy, depressed kind of condition, but it actually is letting go of illusions, which is a goal in our practice.
Disillusion, but not disheartened.
Don't give up.
*Wisdom is a capacity to face uncertain and ambiguous situations with integrity, composure, and reflective insight.* Capacity to face uncertain and ambiguous situations.
Boy, have we got a honey of those kinds of things going on in our world today.
The virus: we don't know really what it's doing or what it will do or how long it will last or what the ultimate effects will be.
We know some things as we're going, we're learning, but we need to live with that uncertainty and that fear.
*Wisdom is not a rule governed capacity.
It does not derive from adherence to a set of rules.* So wisdom comes out of our experience, not out of a guidebook.
*Wisdom is what we call on to decide which rules to bring forth at what time and how to apply them.* This is the Buddhist teaching on skillful means: what to do and when and how.
*Wisdom is the ability to recognize what is and what is not appropriate for dealing with situations skillfully.
Wisdom is speaking and acting at the right time in truth, with affection, and with the mind of goodwill toward all.*
Wisdom allows us to improvise in the moment with skill, not with just whatever comes out of our mouth, but skillfully improvise, respond in the moment to what's needed.
Norman talks about improvising as a component of wisdom, too.
So wisdom in sum is relational.
It is skillfully responding to what is happening now.
It is working with people in situations as they are.
Wearing masks, wearing gloves, washing hands, keeping a distance: that's what our conditions are right now.
When I think of wise people, I also think of people who are naturally good with other people.
They are interested in other people and they get what's happening with other people and they put the other person first.
I've known a few of these magical people in my life.
For me especially, but for a lot of us, it's a study to learn how to do that, to not do it naturally.
And eventually it can be second nature.
So what is the Buddhist teaching on wisdom based on?
Wisdom or understanding?
Norman calls it understanding.
Dale Wright calls it wisdom.
I use those words interchangeably here.
Wisdom develops out of the understanding of emptiness and the basic definitional teachings of Buddhism: no self, impermanence, co-arising.
These are all really difficult concepts to grasp.
And of course, we're not to grasp them, but to find and to really understand.
I'm fascinated by them because there's a whole bunch of them and they're counterintuitive to our Western perspective on reality.
We study them to understand and work with them.
Impermanence means that nothing has an ongoing intrinsic nature.
Nothing that goes on in us or in anything is permanent.
Impermanence is that things are always changing.
Nothing is ever the same from one moment to the next.
Everything is always changing, often imperceptibly, but nonetheless inexorably.
Understanding that emptiness in all things is the foundational step of the Eightfold Path as well.
The first step, if you take it in a line of starting on a path and going, is right view.

It's always interesting to me that right view is probably the most difficult step to get, that you've got to get on that path before you can ever get to understanding what right view is, what the meaning is of Buddhist teachings.
You can practice right speech before you get there.
You can practice right action.
You can practice a whole lot of the steps.
But you do come around again to what is right view.
And right view is made up of these components of emptiness and impermanence and co-arising existence.
Impermanence and emptiness lead to the Buddhist teaching that there is no self, that old difficult thing for us to understand.
How can there be no self when I feel like I'm the same person I've always been?
It means just having no one ongoing nature or set of characteristics, always, always changing.
Phenomena, including us, are always changing.
As soon as we are one thing, in the same moment we are no longer that one thing.
It's instantaneous.
Yes, no.
This, that.
Hard to grasp.
You can't grasp, but that's the point.
It's ungraspable.
You have to somehow sidle up to it and get it for a second.
As soon as we are one thing, we actually are no longer that.
So the teaching also says that self is an illusion.
Even though we identify with ourself, even though it feels like we have or are a continuous self, because we are always changing, we're actually not a self.
Until we understand and accept emptiness of all phenomena, change brings us both misery and relief.
Things we love fade away and pass away, causing us pain.
But things we hate also eventually go away, bringing us relief.
That's always wise to remember, that kind of thing.
It's going to change.
It is changing.
Oh, there it goes.
It went.
The other important aspect about our being empty of an abiding nature is that we are not separate from other beings and entities.
We are instead actually made up of or co-created by our interactions and relationships with others: persons, animals, plants, inanimate objects, whatever our experience is.
We become a combination of that thing, that phenomenon and us, and we change together.
Everything we sense and meet and engage with affects and changes us, so that we are continually recomposed of our experiences with other beings.
We are co-created.
I become partly what each of you experiences me to be, and this is really different for every one of you, and vice versa.
You are what I experience you to be, and that will be different from what others experience you to be.
In our sangha life, we all tumble around together, co-creating each other and ourselves moment by moment, always changing.
Our identity gets exponentially complex very quickly, so much so that our minds really can't hold on to the illusion of having a self.
When you think about it, we can't hold it.
We just naturally let go and just live in the moment for at least a few moments, without labeling or knowing anything cognitively, and in zazen we can do this.
We can approach it or have experiences of realizing there's no form, there's emptiness.
We are it.
This is experiential emptiness.
It's fleeting due to our strongly conditioned reasoning minds, but when it occurs, one has the experience of understanding the nature of things.
It is at such moments that wisdom appears and works.

In Norman's book *The World Could Be Otherwise*, he writes, *the emptiness teachings are truly quite freeing.* These teachings are truly quite freeing in that there's no one thing to hang on to and be confined to.
He goes on, *yes, self is empty.
Constituents of self are also empty.
Nothing exists on its own.
Everything is connection.
Life is ironic.
Things seem to make sense, but they don't.* Things seem to make sense, but they don't.
They're gone already.
It's changed.
There's no point in trying to hang on.
*There is a big joke built into the emptiness teachings, hilarious and tragic at once.*
The joke is hilarious and tragic at once because we can't give up whether we keep wanting it and can't have it.
Quote again from Norman, *taking things too seriously is a sure sign that you have lost the thread of emptiness teachings.
We could call the perfection of understanding or wisdom the perfection of irony.* Taking things too seriously is irony.
Examples of taking things too seriously, all of us have them in our daily life.
Not getting a promotion you're sure you deserved and being unable to get past that for months and months, being upset by it, angry about it.
Or the perennial fight between couples over money or how to discipline the children that goes on year after year after year.
It's hanging on to stuff that's old, maybe legitimate points of view, probably, but not current reality, not current emptiness.
And it causes us all a lot of trouble and pain.
Now we're living in a worldwide pandemic with no predictable end in sight, a dark age lit only by electronic devices that give us the illusion that we are connected.
I'm grateful for this illusion, but I am awed by the enormity of both the pandemic and our human helplessness due to the dislocations we are experiencing.

Although Norman's book was published in 2019, before COVID-19 appeared on the scene, toward the end of the chapter on understanding or wisdom, he includes a commentary on our present cultural dilemma.
I want to read Norman's words as fitting advice to us all.
These quotes are taken from various parts of this chapter, not from contiguous passages.
On page 189 he says, *until fairly recently, human cultures were grounded in absolute eternal truths and values embedded in the religious traditions that provided their unifying ideologies.
When a few centuries ago, open scientific inquiry became compelling, those seemingly eternal truths began to fray.
Revelation based on the mystical testimony of sacred scripture and the hierarchies who interpreted it was no longer a reliable and exclusive source of truth.

A newly competent humanity, no longer subject to the perception of divine control, overthrew such religious truths and strode forward into a new era full of bright possibility.* He goes on, *but recently that confidence has worn thin.
Suddenly the future no longer seems so rosy.*
*We now realize that truth was never really the result of the rational search for meaning we thought it was.
It was always produced by people with social and economic clout to control the message.
Control had simply passed from one hierarchy to another.
Knowing this, we now have [unclear: "worrying culture centers"] whose conflicting notions of what is and should be happening leave us reeling.

The rational give and take of ideas that produce triumphant modernism has become a shouting match* [unclear: "to see why"] there's the need for not being unnerved, or for facing uncertain and ambiguous situations with composure and reflective insight.
We've got lots of opportunities for that now.
Page 190, he goes on, *yet the problem remains, is anything true?
What facts hold up?
Do teachings on the perfection of wisdom or understanding have anything to contribute to this dilemma?
Let's remember that the perfection of understanding or wisdom isn't about understanding something.* Perfection of understanding or wisdom isn't about understanding something.
*It isn't about what we know or even how we know.
It's about who we are and how we navigate this human journey.

Bodhisattvas who practice the perfection of understanding don't necessarily know what's going on, but they have a path through life, a way of being in the world that helps them navigate these choppy waters and a broad set of character traits they have developed through their practice,* that is, through practice of the paramitas, generosity, morality, tolerance, et cetera.
So bodhisattvas don't necessarily know what's going on.
Think of that.
But they have a path through life.
Page 191, *bodhisattvas have the courage to face whatever needs to be faced without retreating into distraction or confusion.
And they trust enough in life to remain hopeful in all conditions, no matter how terrible.
Above all, bodhisattvas are humble.
They understand that all dharmas are empty of own being.
This means that the truth of what goes on, the truth of who one is, is unknown.
It's not that it can be known and we just don't know it yet.
It is beyond knowing.* The truth of who one is is unknown.
It's not that it can be known and we just don't know it yet, that if we keep trying we'll [unclear: "currently"] get there, keep going.
It's beyond our knowing with the frontal brain here.
It's knowing in the body.
*To respect this fact,* Norman says, *is to be humble.* The truth of who one is is beyond knowing.
As we practice being bodhisattvas, as we practice the six paramitas, it is wise to be humble and to reassure ourselves that our emptiness, our no-selfness, is beyond our knowing.
Yet we go on as best we can.
This is prajna, wisdom, without figuring everything out.
We can just be.
I recently participated in a letter writing retreat that was put on in Berkeley and on Zoom, and it was following the program by an organization called Vote Forward.
People write short letters to people in other states to encourage them to vote when voting day comes, and you sign your name and so forth.
So it was a retreat of some zazen and writing and zazen and writing.
And Alan [unclear: "Sanucki"] was the teacher at this.
He's a long, well-regarded teacher from Berkeley and started the Buddhist Peace Fellowship or led it for a long, long time.
Very wise person.
He said in response to someone's question, how do we deal with what's really happening in the world, it's so frightening, he said he titrates the amount of news he takes in daily.
Gets a little, but not so much that it gets him down.
So he manages his news intake.
And then he brings to mind every day the joy, what gives him joy in his life.
So he limits the bad stuff and he focuses on the good stuff.
This helps bring our lives into balance because we can get unbalanced very easily these days.
We don't have to feel guilty about having it better than others do, he said.
If we have homes and food and enough money, we're really lucky and we appreciate that, but we don't have to go and feel guilty.
Our role is to help all beings return to balance, concentrating on the paramitas in our own practice and the emptiness of our being and life.
Back a really long time ago in the Vietnam War, my husband and I had an opportunity to think of a particular statement that was in a line in a poem by John Milton.
John Milton was an English poet in the 17th, 18th century, a very famous poet who wrote *Paradise Lost* and *Paradise Regained*, a religious poet kind of person, a very great one.
He wrote a lot of sonnets and he went blind during his adult life and that was really difficult for him.
So he wrote a sonnet that was called *When I Consider How My Light Is Spent*.
Of course, he didn't have any more light and he couldn't see.
So he was feeling very limited and sorrowful because of that.
But I won't read the whole sonnet.
It's not so long, but it's kind of old English, so it's not so easy to understand.
But he did say,
*God does not need either man's work or his gifts.
His state is kingly, thousands at his bidding speed and post o'er the land and ocean without rest.
They also serve her only stand and wait.*
My husband and I used to say that to each other when we were worrying about Vietnam in about 1967 and '68.
Suddenly American television got into Vietnam and filmed what was happening.
We had never seen these live films before on that war.
And it was really shocking.
It got everybody upset and everybody was out in the streets and so forth.
We also lived in an area in California where we were in a flight pattern for Air Force jets that came over the house.
So I felt like I was in a war zone.
We would see this nightly news and so forth, and there's planes flying over at all hours.
It was a terrifying time.
Not quite like it is now, but very, very active.
So we say that line, *they also serve her only stand and wait.* We serve by being here, by paying attention, by practicing the paramitas and being wise.
Thank you.
There's about maybe 20 minutes if people would like to talk, comment, or Tim, do you think we should go into little groups or?
**Participant:** Well, we could.
It's up to you, a wise speaker.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** A wise speaker, right?
It's kind of like, would you like, do you got anything to say to the whole group or would you rather talk to a couple of people?
Preferences.
**Participant:** I could do kind of bigger groups, like groups of four or five.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Okay.
Can you do that?
**Participant:** Yeah.

So the question: have you had any wise moments lately?
If so, what were they?
What do you struggle with around that?
Not being disheartened, being disillusioned but not disheartened, or any of the other definitions.
Okay, let's spend 10 minutes or so with a group of five-ish and then come back and see if there's anything else to say altogether.
**Participant:** Great, good idea.
I click the go back by mistake.
Well, it's time for that.
Perfect.
Just went back and forward your group, but that's all right.
We're having an interesting conversation about anxiety and panic and the way it's so powerful, but also not real.
And how do you support somebody who's caught by it?
How do you?

Well, we didn't come to any big conclusions, but my main thought was being with them with a sense of compassion, but also the wisdom piece of like, well, it's not maybe as, you know, it is bad, but it's not bad in the way we think it is probably.
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Thank you.
It's a thought, it's changing.
So Tim?

**Participant:** Well, I was just sharing that we were talking a bit about anxiety and panic and that you can be a good supporter for somebody if you can be present and compassionate, you know, feeling that they're suffering, but the wisdom in your own heart is remembering that this isn't permanent or real in that way.
And maybe just your words and deeds and body language will be a little more supportive in a helpful way if you are in touch with the emptiness of suffering, you know?
That's one of the things that came up.
I found it was interesting.
What else did we talk about?
There were three groups?
I think so.
**Participant:** Yeah.
The other group, the second group, somebody with-
**Shuko Edie Norton:** Just a quick check.
Tim, do you want to still be recording?
**Participant:** Oh, no, I'll turn it off.
